prompt.context: The client is a fiber optical manufacturer. Fiber optics are wires that transmit data (internet, TV, phone, etc.). The client sells these wires to large firms like AT&T and Sprint, who put them underground to transmit data over long distances. The CEO of this fiber optical firm is new and is trying to assess the firm's business situation. At a surface level, she knows the firm is experiencing a 50% decline in revenues, but has hired BCG to dig further.
prompt.question: The CEO has three specific questions she wants you to address: (1) Why is the firm experiencing this revenue decline? (2) When will the firm rebound? (3) How does the firm relate to its competition?

clarifying_info.q: What geography should we focus on for the supply/demand analysis?
clarifying_info.a: Use the market of fibers between Washington D.C. and New York as representative of the world for the purposes of this case.

clarifying_info.q: How much fiber capacity exists between D.C. and NY, and what is current peak demand?
clarifying_info.a: There are 1,000 fibers between these two cities, and the peak of demand is 100 terabits/sec. Each fiber can support 1 terabit of information, giving total capacity of 1,000 terabits/sec.
Every year the peak demand doubles. Use time zero as 100 terabits/sec, year 1 as 200 terabits/sec, and so on.

framework: Revenue decline root cause: assess industry-level supply vs. demand dynamics — was too much capacity built relative to actual data demand?
Rebound timing: model demand growth trajectory against installed capacity to find the crossover year when new cable installations will be needed
Competitive positioning: benchmark client against competitors across price, quality, manufacturing capacity, cost structure, market share, customer base, geographic footprint, and balance sheet
Cost structure (ad hoc): use two data points to separate fixed vs. variable costs

questions.prompt: Question 1 — Why is the firm experiencing a 50% revenue decline?
questions.guidance: The revenue decline is industry-wide, not firm-specific. Four years ago, the industry installed far more optical fiber than demand required. Each fiber cable can support about 1 terabit of data, but total demand per second is well below total installed capacity. Supply drastically exceeds demand, pushing revenues down across all players. A strong candidate identifies that this is a structural/industry supply-demand imbalance rather than a competitive or operational failure at the firm level.

questions.prompt: Question 2 — When will the firm rebound? Calculate the year demand will exceed capacity using the D.C.–NY corridor.
questions.guidance: Candidate should set up the demand doubling model against fixed capacity and find the crossover year. Capacity is fixed at 1,000 terabits/sec (1,000 fibers x 1 terabit each). Demand starts at 100 terabits/sec at time zero and doubles each year. The rebound occurs when demand exceeds 1,000 terabits/sec, forcing new installations.

math.setup: Capacity = 1,000 fibers x 1 terabit/fiber = 1,000 terabits/sec (fixed). Demand(t) = 100 x 2^t terabits/sec.
steps: Year 4: demand = 1,600 terabits/sec — exceeds capacity of 1,000
math.answer: Demand exceeds capacity somewhere between Year 3 and Year 4, so the market will rebound in approximately Year 3–4, requiring new fiber installations.

questions.prompt: Question 3 — How does the firm relate to its competition? What dimensions would you compare?
questions.guidance: Candidate should proactively list comparison dimensions before receiving data. Strong answers cover: price, product quality, manufacturing capacity, cost structure, market share, customer base, geographic footprint, and balance sheet / cash position. After the candidate lists dimensions, reveal the firm's profile and push them to identify strategic implications — especially which dimensions matter most in a commoditized, oversupplied market.

questions.prompt: Ad hoc cost structure question — Given two months of production data, determine the firm's variable cost per km and fixed monthly costs.
questions.guidance: Use the difference between the two months to isolate variable cost, then back out fixed costs. A strong candidate sets this up as a two-equation system or uses the marginal approach directly.

math.setup: Month 1: 3MM km produced, total cost = $50MM. Month 2: 2MM km produced, total cost = $40MM.
steps: Variable cost per km = (Cost M1 - Cost M2) / (Volume M1 - Volume M2) = ($50MM - $40MM) / (3MM - 2MM) = $10MM / 1MM km = $10 per km
Fixed costs = Total cost - Variable cost = $50MM - (3MM km x $10/km) = $50MM - $30MM = $20MM per month
math.answer: Variable cost = $10 per km of fiber. Fixed costs = $20MM per month.

recommendation: Revenues have declined because the industry as a whole has declined — current fiber optic supply far exceeds demand, a result of overbuilding approximately 4 years ago.
Based on demand doubling annually, the market will require new fiber installations in approximately 3–4 years (between Year 3 and Year 4).

The client is extremely well-positioned to capture the new demand when it arrives: it has the largest manufacturing capacity, idle capacity ready to deploy, the lowest cost structure, the #1 market share, a stellar customer base (AT&T, Sprint), and a strong balance sheet with cash and no debt.
risks: Demand growth rate could slow below the doubling assumption, pushing the rebound further out
A well-capitalized competitor could preemptively win contracts during the recovery
The prolonged downturn could strain even a cash-rich balance sheet if it lasts longer than projected
next_steps: Monitor demand growth data regularly to refine the rebound timing estimate
Develop a strategy to lock in key customers (AT&T, Sprint) ahead of the capacity crunch
Assess whether selective capacity expansion or acquisitions of distressed competitors make sense during the downturn
